  • Tutorials walk through common tasks, from checking a pilot to exporting a figure.
  • Feature guides explain each part of the app.
  • API & CLI covers the Python API and the command line.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
For sensitive participant data, use the desktop app or run Scanpath Studio on your own machine. Do not upload identifiable recordings to the hosted demo.

Where you run it Where the data is processed desktop app your machine local scanpath-studio your machine hosted demo a Streamlit Community Cloud server operated by Snowflake

docs.title: What happens to a file you upload
docs.text:
Completed datasets, mappings, view settings, and annotations are stored in an on-device recovery cache so a refresh does not erase the session. This happens only when the app listens on this machine alone — the desktop app, or a launch with server.address set to 127.0.0.1, ::1 or localhost — or when you opt in with SCANPATH_STUDIO_PERSIST=1. A server other machines can reach stores nothing: a hosted deployment, and a bare streamlit run, which listens on every interface.

The cache is visible from inside the app: Saved on this computer, at the foot of the Data Management page, reports what is stored, how large it is and the folder it is in, and Clear what is saved… deletes it after a confirmation that lists what goes, then starts the app over. To run without it, start the app with scanpath-studio run --no-persist, or set SCANPATH_STUDIO_PERSIST=0. From a terminal, with the app closed:

scanpath-studio cache                       # what is stored, where, how big
scanpath-studio cache --clear               # delete it
SCANPATH_STUDIO_PERSIST=0 scanpath-studio   # disable recovery storage
SCANPATH_STUDIO_STATE_DIR=/secure/path scanpath-studio   # store it elsewhere

The cache holds the research tables themselves, not just settings — treat that folder like the data files it came from (disk encryption, shared-machine accounts). It is single-user and unencrypted: anyone with your account on that machine can read it.

Exporting an MP4 replay also writes to disk: the encoder needs a real file, so the clip is written to a temporary file in the system's temp folder (readable by your account only) and deleted as soon as it has been read back. Only a crash or a forced kill mid-encode leaves it behind, and it holds the rendered frames, not your tables.

docs.title: The online demo
docs.text: The public demo has no account or data-use agreement. Use it with the bundled sample or data you are comfortable sending to the hosting provider. Sessions are temporary and server resources are limited.

docs.title: What's in a link, a settings file, and an export
docs.text:
• A share link contains the participant and trial IDs plus the visualization settings. It does not contain the data tables — except for a scanpath made with Author a scanpath, whose link carries the typed text and every hand-placed fixation, because they are its data.
  • A settings file ( Share → File) contains the figure's settings and the selected participant and trial IDs — for a comparison, the second trial's participant and trial IDs and its dataset's name too.
  • An annotations file ( Data Management → Annotations, or annotations.json in an Export bundle) contains your notes, which may mention participants.
  • A setup file ( Edit dataset → Download setup file) contains the dataset's name, its column mapping, and its recording setup.
  • An exported table contains the selected research data. A bundle's attached metadata tables hold only the participants, trials and texts it exports.

Review these artifacts before sharing them. Share links can enter browser history, logs, or chat previews, so do not copy one when its participant or trial identifiers should not be exposed there.

docs.title: Network activity
docs.text: Downloading a public corpus contacts its host, and only when you click ⬇ Download — or, headlessly, the first time scanpath-studio render --potec or --onestop (the Public variant) runs against a folder that doesn't have it yet. Check for updates (Help → About, or scanpath-studio version --check) asks GitHub's API (api.github.com) for the latest release, only when you click it; the request carries nothing but the app's version, in its User-Agent. In the desktop app, Update & restart then downloads that release's archive for your computer from GitHub (github.com, which serves the file from its download servers) — only when you click it. The scanpath, animation and comparison figures load the Plotly charting library from the app's own server — the copy installed with the app — so drawing a figure contacts no other host and works without an internet connection, the desktop app included. A figure you download as HTML is different: a saved file has no app server behind it. By default it loads the library from cdn.plot.ly when you open it, which needs an internet connection and tells that host the file was opened (no data travels with the request). Tick Self-contained HTML — shown on the Export subtab once HTML is the chosen format, for the figure, the replay and the bundle — and the HTML embeds the library instead (about 4.8 MB more per file), opens offline and makes no request. HTML written headlessly (save_figure, scanpath-studio render -o figure.html) always embeds it. Streamlit's own usage statistics are switched off on every launch path (scanpath-studio run, the desktop app and the repository's .streamlit/config.toml). The application adds no analytics service of its own.

docs.title: Feature guides
docs.text:
For end-to-end workflows, see the tutorials.

  • Scanpath visualization

    Layers, filtering, replay, and comparison — including across datasets.

  • Data management

    Sources, upload, column mapping, and the recording setup.

  • Corpus Analysis

    Per text, Per participant and Groups, from the measures your data brings.

docs.title: Corpus Analysis
docs.text: Corpus Analysis summarizes many trials at once. It uses the same dataset and trial filters as the Scanpath view. The line beside the dataset picker counts what those filters keep (for example 12 of 24 trials · 1 of 2 participants) and names each active filter. Edit filters opens the Scanpath view's filter panel, and Clear resets every filter.

docs.title: Reading measures come from your data
docs.text: Corpus Analysis shows the reading measures your interest-area report provides (first fixation duration, total fixation duration, regression path, and so on). It does not compute them itself, and without any, the page says so. Which columns count as reading measures is set when the data is loaded (see Reading measures). The per-fixation measures are the fixation table's own durations, and its saccade amplitudes, or, when it has none, the distance between consecutive fixations.

docs.title: Three views
docs.text:
View Answers Per text How was this text read, word by word, across participants? Per participant How does this participant behave across trials? Groups How do conditions or populations differ?

The address bar names the open view (?corpus_subtab=Per+participant), so a bookmark or a copied link reopens it.

Choose a measure, how to aggregate it, and the spread to show. A line under the measure says what it is, its unit, and what each plotted value is (one word, one participant's mean, …), with a link to its definition; a line under the spread says whether it shows how values vary (SD, IQR) or how precisely the center is known (SEM, bootstrap CI). Set a minimum number of participants per word so sparse words don't look like stable estimates.

Groups defines a cohort by splitting on a field, or with its own filters. Turn on Compare a second group, with the two group means and their difference — descriptive, with no significance test. Fields from attached participant, trial or text tables appear here too. A group is a set of whole trials, whichever table holds its field: its word and fixation measures come from the same trials. A trial whose Words and Fixations tables disagree about the field is left out, and the page says so.

docs.title: From summary to evidence
docs.text: Every result table has ⬇ Download this table (CSV), with ⬇ Download the recipe (JSON) beside it: the dataset, trial filters, analysis choices and counts that produced the table, without its rows or any figure settings. When something looks odd, open the trials behind it in the Scanpath view.

docs.title: Choose a dataset
docs.text:
Pick one in the dataset picker above the plot, or on the Data Management page:

  • Bundled demo: a small OneStop sample, for learning the app.
  • Hand-drawn sample: a six-word trial drawn by hand.
  • Public corpus: OneStop or PoTeC, downloaded once when you open it.
  • + → Import files: your own tables.
  • + → Create manually: type a text and place fixations on it by hand.

docs.title: The demo and OneStop
docs.text: The bundled demo is a small part of OneStop Eye Movements, an English eye-tracking-while-reading corpus of 360 participants (Berzak et al., Scientific Data 2025, doi:10.1038/s41597-025-06272-2). The full corpus is four datasets, one per reading regime: ordinary reading, information seeking, repeated reading, and information seeking (repeated). Each downloads from OSF the first time you open it (about 1 GB). A trial is one reading of one paragraph, and its title, paragraph, question, answers and feedback are its screens.

docs.title: What your data needs
docs.text:
Table One row per Needs Fixations (e.g. EyeLink's Fixation Report) fixation trial ID, duration (ms), and x/y or a word ID Words (interest areas) (e.g. EyeLink's Interest Area Report) word trial ID, word ID, and its box: IA_LEFT/RIGHT/TOP/BOTTOM or x/y/width/height Raw gaze gaze sample participant ID, trial ID, x, y Participants (optional) participant participant ID, plus any columns you like Trials (optional) trial trial ID, plus any columns you like Texts (optional) text text ID, plus any columns you like

A dataset needs fixations, words or raw gaze; any one of them is enough, and the others are optional. Participant ID, text ID and timestamps are optional too, and conditions and reading measures unlock more features. Columns are detected from common EyeLink, Gazepoint, Tobii, SMI and Pupil Labs names, and you can correct any guess. Any other column of any table can be kept too (each table's Extra fields to keep): a field with one value per trial, such as a condition, then works as a trial filter, a sort key and a chip above the plot.

docs.title: Files and units
docs.text:
Files can be CSV, TSV, TXT, Parquet, Feather, Excel, or a .zip of any of these. A .zip holding both EyeLink reports (one folder per participant, say) can go in both rows: each row reads only its own reports and says which it left out.

Times are in milliseconds; a header naming another unit ([s], [μs]) is converted. Positions are in pixels: screen fractions are not converted.

docs.title: Metadata tables
docs.text: The participants, trials and texts tables work like columns of your data: they filter trials, appear as chips, sort the trial list, group readers in Corpus Analysis, and are exported beside the data. They are never copied onto the fixations, and a participant missing from the table stays in the data.

docs.title: Trials over several screens
docs.text: A trial shown over several screens maps a screen_id column (and optionally a screen_index for their order) in both tables. Each screen keeps its own coordinates, and the app shows one screen at a time.

docs.title: Reading measures
docs.text: Per-word reading measures (TFD, FFD, first-pass time, regression path…) are columns of the Words table. An EyeLink interest-area report maps them from its IA_* names. Corpus Analysis shows only the measures you mapped and computes none of its own; how each is defined is in Computations & methodology.

docs.title: Add your own data
docs.text:
+ → Import files opens the add dataset screen:

  1. Name the dataset.
  2. Upload the tables. The app autodetects which columns are which: check what it picked, and hover the beside a field to see its first values.
  3. Recording setup: the screen the data was recorded on. Each value starts as an estimate or a default and is labelled so; enter the real screen size, physical width, font size and font if you know them.
  4. Stimulus images (optional, on your own computer): a folder with a screenshot of each text, drawn under the scanpath.

Then click Add dataset. Anything the app cannot use is listed above the button first.

docs.title: The Data Management page
docs.text:
The page lists every dataset with its counts; click a row to open it. Under the list are the open dataset's tables, its annotations, and Data checks, which flag values that cannot be right (such as 0 ms fixations), without removing anything.

The on a row edits the dataset: its name, column mapping, recording setup, stimulus images and metadata tables. Download setup file saves the mapping and setup, so the same files can be added again elsewhere. Nothing changes until you click Save changes. The editor works on the dataset as it was added: only the columns you mapped or chose to keep were stored (the others are listed under dropped at import), so it cannot map a column that was left out. To use one, add the files again.

docs.title: Scanpath visualization
docs.text:
1. Views and Help.
  2. The trial control bar: dataset, trial, screen, sort (⇅) and filter ().
  3. The trial's summary.
  4. The figure.
  5. Plot controls.
  6. Annotations, Stimulus & context, Comparisons, Export and Share.

The Scanpath view draws one reading on the screen it was recorded on.

Looking for a specific button?

All controls lists every button and setting on this view, menu by menu, with a picture of each menu. Search it for what you want to change, such as saccade color or legend position.

docs.title: Choose a trial
docs.text: Pick a trial above the plot. The filter () beside it narrows the list by text, participant, condition or annotation, and ⇅ sorts it. A trial with several screens gets a second navigator to move between them. When several participants have the same trial ID, each reading is in the list on its own, with its participant in brackets, 3 [p2].

docs.title: Control the layers
docs.text:
The Plot controls column holds every setting of the figure. Each layer is one line: a switch, and a ▾ with its settings.

Section What it controls Animate play the reading as a video, at a speed you choose Compare a second reading beside or over this one Design presets restyle the whole figure in one click: Scanpath, Heatmap, Illustration or your last custom settings My designs save the current settings as a design, apply it again in one click, or export it to share or use on another computer Palette one color scheme for the whole figure, such as colorblind-safe or print Fixations markers: size, color, order Saccades lines and arrows, colored by direction or reading type Stimulus text, span highlight, stimulus image, font and background Word boxes each word's interest area: outline and fill, color and opacity Heatmap where fixations concentrate, by count or duration Raw gaze the gaze samples as recorded Filters & highlights which fixations and saccades are drawn, and which stand out Figure & canvas screen framing, axes and grid, title and labels, hover fields, legends

docs.title: Under the plot
docs.text: Tab What it is for Annotations Star, tag and write notes on the trial, to find or filter it later. Stimulus & context The trial's context, such as its title, question and answers, and its highlighted word spans. Comparisons Compare this trial with other trials that match it on a field you choose, such as other readings of the same text, shown side by side. Export Download the figure (PNG, SVG, PDF, HTML) or the video (HTML, GIF, MP4), or a zip bundle of figures and data for many trials. PDF, GIF and MP4 need Chrome, Chromium or Edge installed (FAQ). Share A link that reopens this view (for whoever has the same dataset loaded), the Python or command-line code that redraws the figure, or a settings file.

docs.title: Back up your work
docs.text:
Each of these files can be saved and loaded again:

What Where figure settings Share → File favorites, tags and notes Data Management → Annotations → Export column mapping and recording setup Edit dataset → Download setup file saved figure designs My designs → Export

None of them holds your data, so load the same data before restoring one. On your own computer, the app also keeps your datasets and work between sessions.

docs.title: All controls
docs.text:
Every control on the Scanpath page, where it is and what it does — in the order you meet them on screen. Search this page (Ctrl+F, or Cmd+F on a Mac) for the thing you want to change, such as colors, legends or axes.

The page has two sets of controls:

  • The trial control bar, above the plot, decides what you see: the dataset, the trial, and which trials are in the list.
  • The plot controls, the column on the right, decide how it is drawn: each layer of the figure, its colors and sizes, and the figure as a whole.

The tabs under the plot then work with the trial on screen: annotate it, read its context, compare it, export it or share it. For how the parts fit together, see the Scanpath visualization guide.

docs.title: Trial control bar
docs.text:
The bar above the plot: pick a dataset and a trial, step through the trials, and narrow, sort or label the list.

Control What it does Select dataset The dataset the page shows. + → Create manually Add a dataset by manual illustration: write a text and place its fixations by hand. + → Import files Add a dataset from data tables: upload your own tables as a new dataset. Select trial The trial to show. Click it and type to narrow the list. Trial slider Scrub through the trials in the list. ◀ ▶ The previous or next trial. ⇅ → Sort trials by Reorder the trial list by a statistic (such as reading time), a participant, text or condition field, or a column of a metadata table you attached. ⇅ → Descending Reverse that order. → Text / Participant Keep only these texts or participants. → a field of your data Keep only trials with these values, or, for a number, in this range. → By participant / By trial / By text The same, for the columns of an attached metadata table. → Favorites only Keep only starred trials. → With any of these tags Keep only trials with any of these tags. → Excluding tags Hide trials with any of these tags, such as exclude. → Clear all filters Reset every filter in the panel. ✏️ → Show chips above the plot Show or hide the row of facts about the trial above the plot. ✏️ → field lists Drag fields between Shown and Available to choose the chips. Available holds every field with one value per trial: participant, text and condition columns, the columns of any metadata table you attached, and statistics such as reading time and fixation count. ✏️ → field colors Give a chip a highlight color; its ✕ puts it back to the default gray. ✏️ → Refresh fields Look again for which fields are trial-level. Screen and its ◀ ▶ On a trial recorded over several screens: the screen to show.

docs.title: Plot controls
docs.text: The column on the right of the plot. At the top, the modes and designs change the whole figure at once. Under them, each layer of the figure has a row of its own: the switch turns the layer on or off, and the ▾ beside it opens that layer's settings, described below one menu at a time. The last two rows, Filters & highlights and Figure & canvas, cover the figure as a whole. A greyed-out control says why when you hover over it.

docs.title: Animate: play the reading as a video
docs.text:
The Animate switch turns the figure into an animation, a video of the reading played back fixation by fixation, with play and pause buttons and a time slider under the plot. Its ▾ holds:

Control What it does Replay → Speed How fast the video plays, from ×0.25 to ×8: ×1 is the reader's own pace, ×2 twice as fast, ×0.5 half as fast. Replay → Autoplay → On load Start playing the animation automatically as soon as the plot is shown; otherwise it starts only when you click play. Replay → Duration For information only: the trial's reading time, and how long the video runs at this speed. Frames → Quality How smooth the video is: more frames play more smoothly but take longer to build. Custom sets the two below by hand. Frames → Every Reading time between frames, in ms. Frames → Limit The most frames a video gets; a long trial gets wider frame steps to fit. Frames → Result For information only: how many frames this trial's video has, and how far apart they ended up.

docs.title: Compare
docs.text:
The Compare switch shows a second scanpath, B, beside or over this one (pick it in the trial control bar, above the plot); its ▾ holds:

Control What it does View Overlay both scanpaths, or give each its own panel, Side by side or Top & bottom. Stimulus from In an overlay, whose word boxes and text are drawn: both, A's or B's. Label A / Label B Each scanpath's name in the legend, written with fields such as {participant_id}; empty uses the automatic one. Available fields The fields a label can use. Step → A and B together ◀ ▶ move both scanpaths at once.

docs.title: Design presets and palette
docs.text:
Restyle the whole figure in one click, with a ready-made design or one of your own saved designs:

Control What it does Scanpath / Heatmap / Illustration Ready-made designs: a classic scanpath, a word-box heatmap, or a clean schematic. Custom Your most recent hand-made settings. My designs Your saved designs: click one to apply it; the pencil renames it and the bin deletes it. My designs → save button Save the settings on screen as a named design, to apply again later in one click. My designs → Export / Import Download your designs as a file, or load a file of designs: share a look with co-authors and partners, reproduce a figure exactly, or move your designs to another computer. Palette A color scheme for the whole figure, such as colorblind-safe or print.

docs.title: Fixations
docs.text:
The Fixations switch draws the fixation markers; its ▾ holds:

Control What it does Marker → Color What decides each marker's color. One color paints them all alike. Pick a number column of the fixations, such as duration or the fixation's order in the trial, and the markers follow a color scale: with the default blues, longer fixations show darker. Pick a category, such as the line of text or the next saccade's direction, and each value gets its own color, with a legend. Marker → color box Choose the fixation marker color. Marker → Shape Choose the fixation marker shape: circle, square, diamond, triangle, star… Marker → Size Set the marker size range: the smallest and largest marker diameter, in px. Marker → Scale Choose how duration sets marker size: square root, linear, log, or relative to the trial. Marker → Durations Choose the duration range: set the durations that get the smallest and the largest marker. Marker → Opacity Set the fixation marker opacity; lower it to see overlapping fixations. Marker → Outline Set the width and color of the ring round each marker. Color bar → Show Show the color scale's bar, when markers are colored by a number. Color bar → orientation, Angle, Size, Thickness, Length Set the bar's direction, tick-label angle and size, and its thickness and length. Fixation index → Show Number each fixation in reading order. Fixation index → color, Size Choose the numbers' color and size. Snap → To line Move each fixation onto its line of text — a schematic, labelled Illustration. Snap → Position Choose where on its line a snapped fixation sits.

docs.title: Saccades
docs.text:
The Saccades switch draws the lines between fixations; its ▾ holds:

Control What it does Line → Color Choose what decides the saccade color: one color for all; forward saccades and regressions in two colors; or a color per saccade type (forward, skip, refixation, return sweep, regression), with a legend. Forward / regression and by type need a word ID for each fixation, the word it landed on, mapped in your fixations table (such as EyeLink's CURRENT_FIX_INTEREST_AREA_ID); without one every saccade reads as other. Line → color box Choose the saccade line color. Line → type colors With By type: choose the color of each saccade type, such as regressions or return sweeps. Line → Style Choose the saccade line style: solid, dashed, dotted or dash-dot. Line → Width Set the saccade line width (thickness), in px. Line → Opacity Set the saccade line and arrow opacity; lower it to bring the fixations forward. Shape Choose the saccade shape: straight lines, or arcs over the text (a schematic, labelled Illustration). Direction arrows → Show Show saccade direction arrows: an arrowhead on each saccade, pointing where the eye went. Direction arrows → Arrow size Set the saccade arrowhead size.

docs.title: Stimulus
docs.text:
The Stimulus switch draws the text and the stimulus image; its ▾ holds:

Control What it does Text → Show Show the stimulus text, the words the participant read, at their place on the screen. Fit → Fit to word boxes Size the stimulus text to fill its word boxes, instead of a fixed font size. Spacing Set the stimulus text line spacing: how far apart the lines are, in font sizes. Size Set the stimulus text font size, in px or pt. Font Choose the stimulus text font (typeface); Other… takes any font name. Color → text color Choose the stimulus text color. Background Choose the plot background color: a preset, or any color in the box beside it. Highlight → Show Highlight words in the stimulus text, such as the answer span. Highlight → Highlight words by Choose which words to highlight: a true/false word column, such as the critical span. Style Choose the word highlight style: colored text, or a border round the words; and the highlight color. Image → Show Show the stimulus image, the screen as shown in the experiment, under the scanpath. File Upload a stimulus image (PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP) to draw under the scanpath. Opacity Set the stimulus image opacity; lower it so the scanpath reads over it. Offset → X / Y Move (nudge) the stimulus image left, right, up or down, in px, to line it up with the word boxes. Scale Resize (scale) the stimulus image so its text matches the word boxes.

docs.title: Word boxes
docs.text:
The Word boxes switch draws each word's interest area; its ▾ holds:

Control What it does Box → Line color Choose the word box outline (border) color. Box → Line opacity Set the word box outline opacity; 0 hides the outlines. Box → Fill color Choose the word box fill color, inside each box. Box → Fill opacity Set the word box fill opacity; 0 draws outlines only.

docs.title: Heatmap
docs.text:
The Heatmap switch shows where reading concentrated; its ▾ holds:

Control What it does Style Choose the heatmap style: colored word boxes, a smooth interpolated map, or fixation density. Blur Set the heatmap blur: how far each fixation spreads, for the smooth styles; Auto picks it. Color → By Choose what the heatmap measures: total fixation duration (dwell time), or the number of fixations. Color → Colors Choose the heatmap colors (color scale). Scale Choose a linear or log heatmap scale. Range Set the heatmap color range: the values the colors span. Anything below the range takes the lowest color, and anything above it the highest, so a fixed range keeps colors comparable across trials. Auto fits each trial. Opacity Set the heatmap opacity; Auto uses each style's own. Color bar → Show, orientation, Angle, Size, Thickness, Length Show the heatmap color bar, and set its orientation, label angle and size, thickness and length.

docs.title: Raw gaze
docs.text:
The Raw gaze switch draws the gaze samples as recorded; its ▾ holds:

Control What it does Marker → Color Choose the raw gaze sample color. Marker → Size Set the raw gaze sample marker size. Marker → Opacity Set the raw gaze sample opacity.

docs.title: Filters & highlights
docs.text:
Which fixations and saccades are drawn, and which stand out:

Control What it does Fixations → Index range Show only some fixations: a range of the reading order, such as fixations 10 to 40. Fixations → All trials Keep that fixation range when you move to another trial; otherwise it applies to this trial only, and the next trial shows all its fixations. Short / Long Find short or long fixations by a duration threshold (ms): Highlight marks them, Discard hides them. Out of bounds Highlight or discard out-of-bounds fixations, which land in no word box. Blink Highlight or discard fixations at or next to a blink (needs a blink column). marker and color Choose the marker shape and color of each highlighted fixation kind. Saccades → Types Show only some saccade types, such as regressions or return sweeps. Needs a word ID for each fixation, as for coloring saccades by type.

docs.title: Figure & canvas
docs.text:
The figure as a whole:

Control What it does Frame → Crop to data Crop (zoom) the figure to the part of the screen with data, instead of the whole screen. Margin Set the crop margin: the space round the data when cropping; Auto uses 5%. Border → Show, color Show the border line round the plot area, and choose its color. It marks the edge of the screen, or, with Crop to data, the edge of the cropped area. Grid → Show Show pixel grid lines (a coordinate grid) over the screen. Grid → Auto, interval Set the grid spacing (interval), in px, or let Auto choose it. Labels Set the grid label (tick label) font size. Axes → X / Y Choose the x and y axis fields. X / Y draws the reading on the screen. Any other pair turns the figure into a scatter plot (chart) of the fixations, with no text, word boxes or saccades, keeping the marker colors and sizes. For example: Time (ms) against X for a time course of the reading, where regressions show as dips; Time (ms) against Word # for reading progress through the text; Fixation # against Duration (ms) for fixation durations over the trial. Illustration → Label Choose when to label the figure as a manual illustration, not the recorded positions: when a setting changes its geometry (such as snapping fixations to a line or drawing saccades as arcs), always, or never. Illustration → Text Write the Illustration label's text. Title → Show, text, Size Add a figure title above the plot, and set its font size; {field} inserts a value of the trial. Caption → Show, text, Size, color Add a figure caption below the plot, and set its font size and color. Hover → Words / Fixations Choose the hover fields: what the tooltip shows when the mouse is over a word or a fixation. Legends → Show Show or hide each legend: Compare (A/B), Saccade types, Fixation colors, Size key or Text highlight. Legends → Position Choose the legend position: a corner, the middle of an edge, or down a side, outside or inside the plot. Legends → Arrangement Choose the legend arrangement: items stacked or side by side. Legends → Text size Set the legend text (font) size, in px.

docs.title: Reset visualization
docs.text:
The button at the foot of the column.

Control What it does Reset visualization Reset all plot settings to the defaults. Annotations, filters, data and the selected trial stay.

docs.title: In Compare
docs.text:
With Compare on, scanpath B gets a row of its own, and several menus split into a Scanpath A and a Scanpath B group.

Control What it does Dataset B Choose the dataset scanpath B comes from: this one, or another dataset. Trial B, slider, ◀ ▶ Choose scanpath B's trial: 📄 marks the same text, 👤 the same participant. ⇅ on B's row Sort scanpath B's trial list, apart from A's. By default, trials of the same text as A come first, then the same participant, then the rest; or sort by any field, as on A's row. on B's row Filter scanpath B's trials, apart from A's. Fixations ▾ → Scanpath A / B → Color, Size, Opacity Choose each scanpath's fixation marker color, size range and opacity. Saccades ▾ → Scanpath A / B → Color, Style, Width Choose each scanpath's saccade line color, style and width. Word boxes ▾ → Scanpath A / B → Line, Fill Choose each scanpath's word box outline and fill colors and opacities. Heatmap ▾ → Scanpath A / B → Colors Choose each scanpath's heatmap colors (color scale). Raw gaze ▾ → Scanpath A / B → Color Choose each scanpath's raw gaze sample color. Filters & highlights ▾ → · B groups Set scanpath B's own fixation range, fixation highlights and saccade types.

docs.title: Under the plot
docs.text:
The tabs under the figure:

Tab Control What it does Annotations Favorite Star the trial as a favorite, to find it again with the favorites filter. Tags / Add a tag Tag the trial, with an existing tag or a new one, such as exclude. Tags let you filter the trial list later: the in the trial control bar keeps or hides trials by tag. Notes Write a free-text note on the trial. Stimulus & context Context fields Choose the trial context to show, such as the text's title, a question or an answer. Highlighted spans Choose true/false word columns to highlight in the text, each with a summary. Comparisons Match field Compare with other trials: show the trials that share this trial's value of a field, such as the same text. Columns Set how many comparison panels per row. Export Download format Export (download) the figure on screen as PNG, SVG, PDF or HTML, or the animation as an HTML, GIF or MP4 video. Width, unit, DPI Set the PNG export size for print: width, unit and resolution (DPI). Trials to include Choose which trials to export in the bundle: this one, the filtered trials, or all of them. Formats / Tabular data Choose the bundle's figure formats and the data tables (CSV or Parquet) to include. Separable layers Export each visual layer (fixations, saccades, word boxes…) as its own file, to stack in a vector editor. Annotations (JSON) / Settings file (JSON) Settings file: beside each trial's figure, a plot_config.json recording how it was drawn (layers, colors, sizes, screen, title and caption), so the figures are documented. Annotations: one annotations.json with the exported trials' favorites, tags and notes, which Data Management → Annotations can import again. File path pattern Set the file names inside the export bundle. Build export Build the export bundle (a zip) to download. Share Link Copy a share link that reopens this trial with these settings. The data doesn't travel in the link: whoever opens it needs the same dataset. The bundled demo works anywhere; a public corpus has to be downloaded on their side; for your own dataset, send its files and setup file ( Edit dataset → Download setup file) so they can add it first. A link made on your own computer (a localhost address) opens only where the app runs at that same address. Code → Flavour, Show every option Get the Python or command-line code that redraws this figure, for scripts and reproduction. File → Download settings / Restore settings Save the plot settings to a file, or load (restore) a saved settings file.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Each tutorial walks one research task from start to finish. New here? Start with Install.

  • Optimize data collection

    Pilot your eye tracker, software, and stimulus layout (font, spacing) before you commit — for example, compare two eye trackers on the same text. Catch calibration and setup problems that only show up in a plot, and train new experimenters to spot issues such as frequent blinking, or check their sessions as you supervise.

  • Validate your data

    Mark trials or whole sessions for exclusion, and decide whether you need to collect more. Check that fixation detection and line assignment hold up on this dataset by viewing fixations against the raw gaze and word boxes.

  • Filter data for analysis or publication

    Exclude or flag poorly calibrated, skimming, or non-reading trials, and trials with out-of-bounds, very short, or very long fixations. Annotate trials as you look through them: star them, tag them (such as not reading) or add notes, then filter by those tags. Find the trials a specific analysis needs — for example, participants with a given native language and good calibration — and export the marked trial IDs.

  • Export customized figures

    Show a real scanpath in a paper or talk as a heatmap or a replay, and save the look as a design to reuse. Or bulk-export every trial consistently, for example as training data for models that generate scanpaths on images.

  • Compare and analyze

    Compare model-generated scanpaths with human ones, contrast groups and conditions, and see how reading progresses over time.

The app also has short interactive tutorials under Help → Tutorials. They highlight each control as you go, and never change your data or settings.

docs.title: Analyze a corpus
docs.text:
Move from single scanpaths to a text, condition or group-level result. Each page below is one task.

  • Analyze one text

    How one text was read, word by word, across its readers.

  • Compare groups or conditions

    Two cohorts or conditions side by side, with their difference.

  • See progression over time

    How reading changes over a session, for a participant or a group.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Corpus Analysis shows the reading measures your interest-area table brings (mapped under Reading measures when you add or edit a dataset); it computes none itself. The bundled demo has them. With fixations alone, compute the measures with your own pipeline (EyeLink Data Viewer's interest-area report, for example), join them onto your Words (interest areas) table by participant, trial and word ID, and load that; EyeLink's IA_* names map themselves.

Define the pool. Narrow the trials with the Scanpath view's filter or Edit filters at the top of Corpus Analysis. The line beside the dataset picker there counts the trials and participants left and names each active filter; Clear resets them. A text ID must identify the same stimulus across participants; a trial ID identifies one trial.

docs.title: Keep the result
docs.text: Select Download this table (CSV) beside a result, and Download the recipe (JSON) beside it. The recipe records how the table was made: the app version, the dataset's name, the trial filters, the view's text, screen, measure, aggregation, normalization, spread, minimum participants and group definitions, and the trial and participant counts. It names the dataset rather than copying it, and holds no figure settings. A Share link carries neither the filters nor the Corpus Analysis choices.

docs.title: Analyze one text
docs.text:
How was one text read — which words drew long fixations, and how do its readers differ?

  1. Define the pool, then open Corpus Analysis → Per text and pick the text.
  2. Choose one familiar measure: total fixation duration for overall attention, first-pass reading time for initial processing, or regression rate for rereading.
  3. Read the word profile on the stimulus, or against a word property such as surprisal. Set a minimum number of participants per word, so isolated observations do not appear as stable estimates.
  4. Check how many participants contribute, and open a scanpath view to investigate surprising words.

One text's total fixation duration on the stimulus and then against GPT-2 surprisal.

Then: download the table and its recipe.

docs.title: Compare groups or conditions
docs.text:
Do two populations or conditions read differently?

  1. Define the pool, then open Corpus Analysis → Groups.
  2. Define one cohort — split a field, or build a filter set — and check that it looks right.
  3. Turn on comparison, define the second cohort, and read Group means & difference. It compares the two cohorts' per-participant means and is descriptive: there is no significance test.
  4. Read it with its denominator: the caption says how many participants are in each cohort and how many are in both. A participant in both contributes to both means, and then the standardized difference is not shown — see how it is computed.

The same measure's distribution in two groups, the Adv and Ele texts (at the end of the recording).

Then: download the table and its recipe.

docs.title: See progression over time
docs.text:
Does reading change as a session goes on — with fatigue, practice, or as a condition takes effect? In Corpus Analysis:

Question View How does one participant's reading change over the session? Per participant → Per-trial trend How do their fixation durations change over the session? Per participant → Fixation duration over time How does a group's reading change over time? Groups → Group trend

The trend follows the trials in the order your data's trial index records, so map that column when you add the dataset. Narrow the pool first to the participants or condition the question is about — see Before you start — and keep the result as in Keep the result.

docs.title: Optimize data collection
docs.text:
Problems in eye-tracking data are cheapest to fix before and during collection. Use Scanpath Studio to:

  • pilot your setup: your eye tracker and software, and the stimulus layout (font, spacing), before you commit to them;
  • check that the setup is correct: calibration problems often only show up in a plot of the data, and during collection the data moves too fast to see every issue;
  • train and supervise experimenters: problems such as a participant blinking often are hard to notice live but easy to see in the plots, so new experimenters can learn from them and the person overseeing collection can check each session.

Each page below is one task, with recordings of it in the app.

  • Check a session

    Check a pilot or completed session for setup, calibration and recording problems, and record what you find.

  • Compare two eye trackers

    Record the same text with two trackers, or two setups, and compare.

  • Audit an experimenter

    Review one experimenter's sessions, or compare two experimenters'.

For a formal retained and excluded pool afterwards, continue with Filter data.

docs.title: Audit an experimenter
docs.text:
When several people run sessions, check each experimenter's work: whether their participants are calibrated well, and whether problems recur in their sessions.

You need to know which experimenter ran each session. Keep that as a column in your data (under Extra fields to keep when you add the dataset), or as a column of a participants table (Metadata → Participants). Either way it becomes a filter in the trial picker's filter funnel — a data column among the conditions, a participants-table column under By participant.

docs.title: Review one experimenter's sessions
docs.text:
1. Open the filter funnel beside the trial picker and pick the experimenter.
  2. Step through their trials with ◀ ▶, and replay the ones that look wrong.
  3. In Annotations, tag what you find, such as calibration or blink, with the experimenter's name in the note, so the review is one export away.

Narrowing the trial list by a condition and one participant — the same funnel narrows it to one experimenter.

docs.title: Compare two experimenters
docs.text:
1. Turn on Compare.
  2. Narrow scanpath A's trials to one experimenter, and scanpath B's — with the filter funnel on B's own row — to the other.
  3. Pick trials of the same text, marked 📄, and compare how the two sets of recordings look: precision, missing stretches, drift.

Save what you found as in Check a session.

docs.title: Check a session
docs.text: Check a pilot or completed session for setup, calibration and recording problems, and leave a record of which trials need attention and why.

docs.title: 1. Load the session
docs.text:
On the Data Management page select Add dataset → Import files, upload the Words (interest areas) and Fixations tables, then check the proposed columns and the Recording setup — the monitor resolution the session was actually recorded at — before selecting Add dataset. If the dataset is already loaded, click its row in the list of datasets.

Adding the bundled demo's EyeLink fixation and interest-area reports: the columns are detected, and the recording setup arrives filled in.

docs.title: 2. Check the setup on one trial
docs.text:
Keep the default view first, then turn on Word boxes and confirm that:

  • the word boxes match the displayed text;
  • fixations fall on or near words rather than off the screen;
  • the first and last fixations look plausible.

If every trial is shifted in the same way, the problem is the setup, not the participant: check the monitor size in the Recording setup and the coordinate system.

docs.title: 3. Replay the recording
docs.text:
A still scanpath hides timing. Turn on Animate and look for long missing periods, repeated points out of bounds, frequent interruptions such as a participant blinking often, or a vertical shift that grows during the trial — a sign of calibration drift.

To make these stand out, open Filters & highlights → Fixations in the plot rail and Highlight short, long or out-of-bounds fixations. Highlighting keeps the whole trial visible; keep Discard for a later, documented filtering decision.

Replaying a trial fixation by fixation, then at four times real time.

docs.title: 4. Record what you find
docs.text:
Open Annotations under the plot: star a good example, add a tag such as calibration, blink, setup or review, and write one sentence describing the evidence and the action. Move through the participant's trials with the trial picker.

Starring a trial and tagging it, starring another, then showing only the starred ones.

docs.title: 5. Save the review
docs.text:
Open Data Management → Annotations and select Export. The file keeps your stars, tags and notes; Share → File keeps the view settings beside it. To return to a trial from its note, select Open on its row there.

Done: you have checked geometry and timing, marked the trials that need attention, and saved the review. For a formal retained and excluded pool, continue with Filter data.

docs.title: Compare two eye trackers
docs.text:
Choosing between two eye trackers, or two recording setups, for an experiment? Record the same text with each and compare the scanpaths.

  1. Load each recording as its own dataset, each with the Recording setup of the screen it was recorded on.
  2. Open the first tracker's dataset and select a trial.
  3. Turn on Compare. In scanpath B's row, choose the second tracker's dataset under Dataset B, then a trial of the same text — trials of the same text are marked 📄.
  4. Compare the two readings: precision, how fixations sit on the words, missing stretches. Recordings on screens of the same size can be overlaid; otherwise each is drawn on its own screen, side by side. Turn on Animate to replay both on one clock.

Two readings of the same text, overlaid and then side by side. Here both come from the demo; with two trackers, scanpath B comes from the second tracker's dataset.

The same steps compare two stimulus layouts, such as two fonts or line spacings, when each was recorded as its own dataset.

docs.title: Filter data
docs.text:
Decide which trials an analysis or a publication should use, and leave a record anyone can audit — without changing the data itself. Each page below is one task.

  • Exclude unsuitable trials

    Mark poorly calibrated, skimming or non-reading trials and leave them out.

  • Select participants by a field

    Keep, for example, the native speakers of one language with good calibration, and export their trial IDs.

  • Find the trials an analysis needs

    Trials with out-of-bounds, very short or very long fixations, or many blinks.

docs.title: How the filters work
docs.text: Open the filter funnel beside the trial picker: it holds the text and participant pickers together with the condition and annotation filters. A condition filter decides each trial as a whole, from whichever table holds the field: a difficulty level recorded only in your Words table narrows the fixations too. A trial whose Words and Fixations tables give it different values is left out, and a warning above the plot names it. If the pool becomes empty, the app names the filter that emptied it and offers to clear just that one.

docs.title: Every task ends the same way
docs.text:
Check the pool. Look at one trial from each participant or condition, then confirm on the Data Management page that the counts under What's in … → Stats are plausible. They follow the filters; the dataset table above them counts the whole dataset.

Export it. Use Export → Export bundle for the active filtered pool, with the tidy tables, plot_config.json and Annotations (JSON). The bundle's index.csv lists the participant and trial of every trial it exported.

Building a zip of every trial's figures and tables (the build is fast-forwarded).

Keep the record. Export the annotations from Data Management → Annotations → Export: each entry names its participant and trial with its star, tags and note, including trials a filter now hides. (The bundle's annotations.json covers only the trials it exports.) The original data stays intact.

docs.title: Exclude unsuitable trials
docs.text: Mark the trials that should not be analysed — poorly calibrated, skimming, or not reading at all — and leave them out of the pool without deleting them.

docs.title: 1. Review each trial
docs.text: Inspect the default scanpath, and turn on Animate when timing helps: skimming shows as long jumps and few fixations, poor calibration as fixations shifted off the lines. Open Filters & highlights → Fixations in the plot rail and Highlight out-of-bounds fixations; highlighting keeps the whole trial visible.

docs.title: 2. Tag the decision
docs.text:
In Annotations, apply a consistent tag vocabulary — for example exclude, poor-calibration or skimming — and add a brief reason.

Starring a trial and tagging it, starring another, then showing only the starred ones.

docs.title: 3. Leave the tagged trials out
docs.text:
First save the full record ( Data Management → Annotations → Export). Then, in the filter funnel under By trial annotation, put exclude in Excluding tags — not in With any of these tags, which would keep only the rejected trials. The pool is now the trials you kept.

On a dataset with several screens per trial, a tag on a single screen does not hide its trial; find those on Data Management → Annotations.

Then: check and export the pool.

docs.title: Find the trials an analysis needs
docs.text: Some analyses need particular trials: ones with very short or very long fixations, fixations out of bounds, or many blinks.

docs.title: 1. Make them stand out
docs.text: Open Filters & highlights → Fixations in the plot rail and Highlight the category you are after: Short or Long (each with its own threshold in ms), Out of bounds (fixations in no word box), or Blink (fixations at or next to a blink — it needs a blink column in your data).

docs.title: 2. Bring them to the top
docs.text: Use the ⇅ trial-ordering popover beside the trial picker to sort the trials, for example by reading time to surface unusually short or long ones, and step through them with ◀ ▶.

docs.title: 3. Mark them
docs.text:
Tag the trials the analysis needs in Annotations, then keep only them: in the filter funnel under By trial annotation, put the tag in With any of these tags.

Then: check and export the pool.

docs.title: Select participants by a field
docs.text: Keep the participants an analysis is about — for example, the native speakers of one language whose calibration is good — and export their trial IDs.

docs.title: 1. Attach a participants table
docs.text: Native language, age or a questionnaire score is recorded per participant, not per trial. Attach a participants table, one row per participant: under Metadata → Participants when you add the dataset, or later in Data Management → Edit dataset → Data tables & column mapping.

docs.title: 2. Filter on it
docs.text:
Its columns appear under By participant in the filter funnel. Pick the language, and the trial picker keeps only those participants' trials.

Narrowing the trials to one condition and one participant: from 24 trials to 6 — participant fields narrow the same way.

docs.title: 3. Check their calibration and mark the trials
docs.text: Step through the remaining trials and tag the ones to keep, such as include, or the ones to drop — see Exclude unsuitable trials.

docs.title: 4. Export the trial IDs
docs.text:
Export the annotations ( Data Management → Annotations → Export): each entry names its participant and trial. Or export the filtered pool as a bundle, whose index.csv lists every trial in it.

Then: check and export the pool.

docs.title: Export customized figures
docs.text:
Show a real scanpath in a paper, a talk or a supplement — or export a consistent image set for downstream processing, such as training data for models that generate scanpaths on images. Each page below is one task.

  • Export one figure

    A scanpath or a heatmap for a paper or a talk, at the size the page needs.

  • Export a replay

    The animated reading as a GIF, an MP4 or an interactive page.

  • Export every trial

    The same view across many trials, with its provenance.

docs.title: Export a replay
docs.text:
The reading as it happened, for a talk or a supplement.

  1. Choose the view as for one figure, then turn on Animate and set the speed.
  2. Open Export → Current figure: the replay saves as HTML (interactive, with its own play controls), GIF or MP4. GIF and MP4 need Chrome, Chromium or Edge; the clip runs as long as the replay plays at its speed.

Rendering the replay to a GIF and downloading it; the wait while it renders is fast-forwarded.

docs.title: Export every trial
docs.text: The same view across many trials — for a supplement, or as a consistent image set for downstream processing.

docs.title: 1. Set the view once
docs.text: Choose the view as for one figure; every trial in the batch is drawn with it.

docs.title: 2. Build the bundle
docs.text:
In Export → Export bundle:

  1. choose this trial, the active filtered pool, or the whole dataset;
  2. select figure and table formats;
  3. preview the filename pattern;
  4. start the export and inspect one file before using the batch.

For post-production, enable separable layers so text, boxes, fixations, saccades, heatmap, and stimulus image can be stacked in a vector editor.

Adding PNG and the fixation and word-measure tables, then building a zip of all 24 trials (fast-forwarded) and downloading it.

docs.title: 3. Keep provenance
docs.text:
Keep plot_config.json with the batch. The bundle's README.md records the package version and which trials it was built from, and index.csv lists every file with its participant, trial and screen, and any that failed. Record the dataset version and the trial filters you used in the caption or analysis log — the export does not store them.

Done: the exported files share one visual configuration and can be recreated. For scripted runs, see Automation.

docs.title: Export one figure
docs.text: A real scanpath for a paper or a talk — as a scanpath, a heatmap or a comparison — at the size the page needs.

docs.title: 1. Choose the view
docs.text:
Set the monitor size first, under Data Management → Edit dataset → Recording setup; it defines the figure's coordinate system. Then choose the participant and trial, and keep only the layers that answer the question:

  • Fixations + saccades + text for a conventional scanpath;
  • Heatmap + text for spatial concentration;
  • Compare for two trials of the same text.

The design presets set a whole view in one click — Scanpath, Heatmap, Illustration — and every layer stays adjustable from there.

One click for each design: Heatmap, Illustration and Scanpath, then a heatmap added to the scanpath.

docs.title: 2. Make it clean
docs.text: Check the whole canvas for clipped marks, unreadable text, and an unnecessary legend. When several figures must share identical grid marks, set a manual interval under Figure & canvas → Axes & grid → Grid (untick Auto).

docs.title: 3. Export it
docs.text:
Open Export → Current figure and choose:

Need Format editable vector SVG or PDF image for slides/web PNG interactive inspection HTML

PNG and SVG are saved by your browser from the figure on screen, and HTML needs nothing either (it loads Plotly from the internet when opened, or tick Self-contained HTML for a larger file that opens offline); PDF needs Chrome, Chromium or Edge. For print, give the PNG a Width (mm or in) and a DPI: 180 mm at 600 dpi is 4,252 px wide, and Share → Code writes the same size. Without a width, the plot's own camera button saves the same PNG.

Setting the width to 180 mm at 300 dpi and downloading the PNG.

docs.title: 4. Save the look for next time
docs.text: To give the next figure the same look, save its settings as a design: open My designs in the plot rail and select its save button. A saved design applies the same layers, colors and sizes to any trial in one click. Export writes your designs to a file, and Import reads one back on another computer or shares them with a colleague.

docs.title: 5. Keep it reproducible
docs.text:
Under the plot, Share keeps the figure reproducible: Link reopens the app on this trial with these settings, Code writes the Python or command line that redraws it, and File saves the settings to load again later.

Looking at the code that redraws the figure, then copying a link that reopens the same trial with the same design.
